game_world: a fantasy RPG (think Zelda or Stardew Valley)
title: Data Types: Your RPG Hero Sheet Comes to Life
tagline: Forge your fantasy hero from scratch — every stat, every item, every name — and watch your RPG character sheet light up the terminal!
scratch_bridge: In Scratch, you used variables to store things like a score or a player's name, and Scratch automatically figured out whether it was a number or words for you. In Python, YOU get to choose the type of data you store — which gives you way more power, like the difference between a wooden sword and a legendary enchanted blade.

concept.plain_english: Every piece of information in your game has a TYPE — think of it like the category on your RPG character sheet. Your hero's name is TEXT (called a string), their health points are a WHOLE NUMBER (called an integer), their speed multiplier might be a DECIMAL NUMBER (called a float), and whether they have a shield equipped is TRUE or FALSE (called a boolean). Python needs to know what TYPE of data it is so it knows what to do with it — you can't add a name to a number, just like you can't add your hero's name to their HP stat! Each type unlocks different powers: you can do math with numbers, combine text, and make yes/no decisions with booleans.
concept.why_it_matters: Once you understand data types, you can build a real character creation screen where players type their hero's name, choose their class, and see a fully formatted stats sheet printed to the screen.
concept.analogy: Data types are like the different slots on an RPG character sheet — the Name slot only accepts text, the HP slot only accepts a number, the Shield Equipped slot only accepts Yes or No, and the Attack Multiplier slot accepts decimals. Each slot has rules about what goes in it!

code_example.title: hero_sheet.py
code_example.code:
# === HERO CHARACTER SHEET ===
hero_name = "Aelindra"          # string: text in quotes
hero_level = 5                   # integer: whole number
hero_hp = 100                    # integer: whole number
hero_attack_multiplier = 1.75    # float: decimal number
hero_has_shield = True           # boolean: True or False

print("╔══════════════════════════╗")
print("║    ⚔️  HERO CHARACTER SHEET  ⚔️   ║")
print("╠══════════════════════════╣")
print(f"║  Name   : {hero_name:<17}║")
print(f"║  Level  : {hero_level:<17}║")
print(f"║  HP     : {hero_hp:<17}║")
print(f"║  Atk x  : {hero_attack_multiplier:<17}║")
print(f"║  Shield : {str(hero_has_shield):<17}║")
print("╚══════════════════════════╝")
code_example.explanation: Line 1 is just a comment — your notes to yourself, like sticky notes on your code. Line 2: hero_name is a STRING — any time data is wrapped in quotes, it's a string, which is Python's word for text. In Scratch, this is like setting a variable to 'Aelindra' using a Set block. Line 3: hero_level is an INTEGER — a plain whole number, no quotes, no decimal. Line 4: hero_hp is another integer. Line 5: hero_attack_multiplier is a FLOAT — that just means a number with a decimal point, like 1.75x attack power. Line 6: hero_has_shield is a BOOLEAN — it's either True or False, exactly like a Scratch boolean (the pointy diamond-shaped blocks!). Lines 8-16 are the magic — we're printing a fancy box using special characters, and f-strings (the f before the quote) let us plug our variables right into the text, like how Scratch lets you join words and variables together. The :<17 part just makes everything line up neatly in the box. BOOM — you just printed a real RPG character sheet!

exercises.game_context: You are building the tavern welcome screen that greets a new adventurer when they start the game.
exercises.title: The Tavern Welcome Board
exercises.instructions: Step 1 — Create four variables for a brand new hero: their name (a string, your choice!), their starting gold (an integer, try 50), whether they are a member of the Adventurers Guild (a boolean, True or False), and their luck stat as a decimal like 0.85. Step 2 — Print a tavern-style welcome sign using those variables. The sign should show all four pieces of info inside a border made of characters like = or * or +. Step 3 — Make sure each data type appears at least once so the tavern board shows a name, a number, a decimal, and a True/False value. Your output should look like a real in-game notice board nailed to the tavern wall!
exercises.starter_code:
# === TAVERN WELCOME BOARD ===
# Step 1: Create your hero's starting info
adventurer_name = "???"       # string: put your hero's name here
starting_gold = 0             # integer: how much gold do they start with?
guild_member = False          # boolean: are they in the guild?
luck_stat = 0.0               # float: their luck as a decimal

# Step 2: Print the welcome board
# Hint: use print() for each line and f"...{variable}..." to plug in your values
print("+================================+")
# YOUR CODE HERE
exercises.hint: Remember: strings need quotes around them like 'Borin Ironboot', integers are just plain numbers like 50, floats have a decimal point like 0.85, and booleans are exactly True or False with a capital letter. To plug a variable into your print, use f"Hello {variable_name} !" — that's called an f-string and it's like Scratch's join block!
exercises.scratch_equivalent: In Scratch, this is like using a Set [variable] to [value] block for each stat, then using Say blocks with join to display them all together on screen.

exercises.game_context: You are building the pre-battle stats comparison screen that appears right before your hero fights a dungeon boss.
exercises.title: Boss Battle Stats Showdown
exercises.instructions: Step 1 — Create variables for YOUR HERO: name (string), hp (integer), attack (integer), is_poisoned (boolean, set to False). Step 2 — Create variables for THE BOSS: name (string, something scary!), hp (integer, make it bigger than yours!), attack (integer), is_enraged (boolean, set to True). Step 3 — Print a side-by-side battle screen with both sets of stats inside a cool border. Step 4 — Below the stats, use an if statement to print a warning line: if the boss hp is greater than your hp, print a warning message like DANGER: Boss outmatches you! otherwise print ADVANTAGE: You have more HP! Step 5 — At the bottom, calculate and print total_power for your hero as attack multiplied by 10, to show what damage they could deal. Make sure your output looks like a real RPG battle intro screen!
exercises.starter_code:
# === BOSS BATTLE STATS SCREEN ===

# YOUR HERO — fill these in!
hero_name = "Lyra Swift"     # string
hero_hp = 80                  # integer
hero_attack = 25              # integer
hero_is_poisoned = False      # boolean

# THE BOSS — make them scary!
boss_name = "???"             # string: give the boss a name
boss_hp = 0                   # integer: make this bigger than hero_hp!
boss_attack = 0               # integer
boss_is_enraged = True        # boolean

# Step 3: Print the battle screen
print("╔════════════════════════════════════╗")
# YOUR CODE HERE — add more print lines for the full screen

# Step 4: HP comparison — use an if statement!
# if boss_hp > hero_hp:
#     print("...")
# else:
#     print("...")

# Step 5: Calculate total power (integer math!)
total_power = hero_attack * 10
# print it out!
exercises.hint: For the side-by-side layout, each print line handles one row of the table — just put both heroes info in the same print statement separated by the border character. Remember that multiplying two integers gives you another integer, which is perfect for the power calculation. The if statement works exactly like Scratch's if-then-else block — if the condition is True, it runs the first chunk, otherwise the second!
exercises.scratch_equivalent: In Scratch, this is like using multiple Set variable blocks to build up all your stats, then using if-then-else blocks with the green operator blocks (like greater than >) to compare them, and Say blocks to display the result.

quiz.question: Your hero picks up a magical sword named 'Dawnblade'. You want to store the sword's name in Python. Which data type do you use?
options: A) integer — because it's a whole thing
B) string — because it's text, wrapped in quotes
C) boolean — because the hero either has it or doesn't
D) float — because swords have weight
quiz.explanation: A string is the data type for any text — words, names, sentences. Whenever you're storing something you would type out in letters, like a sword name or a hero's title, you wrap it in quotes and Python knows it's a string. The sword's NAME is text, so string is the perfect slot on the character sheet for it!

quiz.question: Your hero's health is at 73 HP. Later it drops by half to 36.5 HP. Which data types would you use for these two HP values?
options: A) Both are strings because HP is displayed on screen
B) 73 is an integer, and 36.5 is a float because it now has a decimal
C) Both are booleans because health is either full or empty
D) Both are floats because numbers are always floats in games
quiz.explanation: 73 is a whole number with no decimal, so it's an integer — think of it as a clean whole HP bar. But 36.5 has a decimal point, which makes it a float. In many RPGs you keep HP as integers, but some games (like ones with percentage-based damage) need floats for precise damage calculations. Knowing the difference lets you choose the right tool!

quiz.question: You're coding a checkpoint system. The player either HAS reached the dungeon checkpoint or they HAVEN'T. What is the perfect data type to store this?
options: A) string — store it as 'yes' or 'no' in quotes
B) integer — use 1 for yes and 0 for no
C) boolean — store it as True or False
D) float — use 1.0 for reached and 0.0 for not reached
quiz.explanation: Boolean is MADE for exactly this — any time something in your game is a yes/no, on/off, or has/doesn't have situation, boolean is your best friend. checkpoint_reached = True is clean, readable, and tells Python to treat it as a true/false decision. You might have seen this in Scratch as the pointy diamond-shaped blocks that only hold true or false — same idea in Python!

challenge.title: RPG Character Creation Screen
challenge.game_context: You are building the character creation screen that every player sees when they boot up your fantasy RPG for the first time.
challenge.description: Using everything from this lesson, build a full character creation display. Create at least 6 variables covering ALL FOUR data types (string, integer, float, boolean). Include: the hero's name and class (strings), their starting HP and gold (integers), their critical hit chance as a percentage decimal like 0.15 (float), and two boolean flags like has_magic and is_veteran. Then print a gorgeous multi-section character sheet with: a header banner, a stats section with a visual HP bar made of block characters, an equipment section, a traits section showing the booleans, and a footer showing their calculated power rating (hp multiplied by critical hit chance, rounded to 1 decimal). Make it look like something you'd actually see in a real RPG — go wild with the border characters!

encouragement: You just coded real data types — the exact same building blocks that the developers of Stardew Valley used to track every crop timer, every villager's friendship level, and every item in your backpack. With strings, integers, floats, and booleans in your toolkit, you have everything you need to start building your own RPG inventory system, a battle engine, or even a full character creator — the dungeon is yours to conquer!
